seo.title: Karmic tail 12 16 22 compatibility: Hanged Man, Tower and Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 16 22 compatibility exists only for a couple: no single birth date can produce it. What The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Fool say about two people.

title: Karmic tail 12-16-22 in compatibility: two people after the flood
short: No single birth date can produce the triple 12-16-22. For this tail to be personal, The Star would have to sit in the centre of the chart, and The Star never appears in the centre of a personal destiny matrix. This tail and this Star exist only for two people — and they tell how a couple waits things out together, goes through a collapse together and learns together to start from nothing.

sections.h2: Two people on Parnassus: the story of the 12-16-22 tail
paragraphs: Ovid finished the Metamorphoses around 8 AD. The first book begins with the creation of the world and almost at once drowns it. Quotations follow Henry T. Riley's literal prose translation of 1851.

Jupiter, disguised as a man, walks the earth and enters the house of Lycaon, king of Arcadia. Lycaon decides to test his guest: "I will make trial, by a plain proof, whether this is a God, or whether he is a mortal." The test turns out to be a trap, and the answer to it is lightning: "I, with avenging flames, overthrew the house upon the household Gods, worthy of their master." Lycaon flees to the fields and becomes a wolf.

One house is not enough for Jupiter: "Thus fell one house; but one house alone did not deserve to perish." He is ready to scatter his thunderbolts over the whole earth, but fears setting the sky on fire, lays them aside and chooses water. Ovid's flood is a world turned upside down. A man "catches a fish on the top of an elm-tree", an anchor is fastened in a green meadow, dolphins get into the woods, the wolf swims among the sheep, and "the towers tottered, overwhelmed beneath the stream". In the end "everything now was ocean; and to that ocean shores were wanting".

One mountain stays above the water: "a lofty mountain rises towards the stars, with two tops, by name Parnassus". Here Deucalion comes to rest, "borne in a little ship, with the partner of his couch". Jupiter sees that of so many thousands one man and one woman are left, "both guiltless, and both worshippers of the Gods", and stops the flood.

Then begins the part a couple should read this myth for. Deucalion looks at the empty earth and weeps: "O sister, O wife, O thou, the only woman surviving… we two are the whole people of the earth, whatever both the East and the West behold." The two go to the river, sprinkle themselves with its water and ask the goddess Themis for advice. The answer is a riddle: "cover your heads, and loosen the garments girt around you, and throw behind your backs the bones of your great mother." Pyrrha refuses: she is afraid to offend her mother's shade. Deucalion finds another reading: the great mother is the earth, her bones are stones. Neither of them is sure. "But what harm will it do to try?" The two throw stones behind their backs, and slowly the stones become people.

The order of the cards is the order of their own path. The entry is a boat over an upturned world, where the two have nothing but each other (12). The middle is the land where everything has fallen, and a word that must not be taken literally (16). The main task is a step with no safety net, taken with covered heads (22).

sections.h2: The Hanged Man — entry to the task: "we two are the whole people of the earth"
paragraphs: In Yuliana Lisovskaya's book on compatibility, point M is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". It stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. For the 12-16-22 couple, the common language is the language of The Hanged Man.

It is heard best in Deucalion's speech on the empty earth. It is a declaration of love made through sacrifice: "What would now have been thy feelings, if without me thou hadst been rescued from destruction, O thou deserving of compassion? In what manner couldst thou have been able alone to support this terror? With whom for a consoler, to endure these sorrows? For I, believe me, my wife, if the sea had only carried thee off, should have followed thee, and the sea should have carried me off as well." In Waite's list of meanings for The Hanged Man, "wisdom, circumspection" stand next to "trials, sacrifice". Deucalion speaks this language: I am with you, even if it means death.

In a living couple, this entry shows in small things. The two give up their own plans for each other with ease: one does not go where they have long wanted to go, so as not to leave the other alone. They are happy together, away from people, and they sense each other at a distance. Big decisions wait "for better times". Lisovskaya writes that such a couple needs a push from outside even to marry. Ovid's push is the strongest one possible: the rest of the world has gone under water.

The Hanged Man is the card of the inverted view, and Ovid turns the whole world upside down: a fish in the treetop, an anchor in the grass, sea-calves where goats used to graze. The couple enters its task in a world where everything familiar stands on its head, and the two hold on to each other because there is nothing else to hold. In Apollodorus (Library, I.7.2) the boat is a chest built on Prometheus's advice, and the two spend "nine days and as many nights" floating in it over the sea. That is The Hanged Man: life suspended, but life.
Benebell Wen assigns The Hanged Man to the element of Water. In this couple's myth, the entry to the task is literally water.

The flood is over, yet Deucalion is still afraid: "And even now there is no certain assurance of our lives; even yet do the clouds terrify my mind." The danger has passed; the waiting has stayed. This is the minus of entry 12: a couple who came through something together keeps waiting long after there is nothing left to wait for.

There is a second minus too — someone else's voice inside the couple. Pyrrha refuses to follow the goddess's advice: she "dreads to offend the shades of her mother by casting her bones". Among the minuses of The Hanged Man, Lisovskaya lists parents' power over the couple, decisions made "because that's how it's done" and worry about what people will say. Deucalion, without noticing, adds one more weight: "Thus it has seemed good to the Gods, and we remain as mere samples of mankind." A model couple has to be a proper couple — and it finds it hardest of all to say aloud what each of the two wants.

paragraphs.h3: The Moon and The World in one entry

paragraphs: In every 12-16-22 couple the entry is built the same way: one partner's personal tail begins with The Moon (18), the other's with The World (21), and 18 + 21 = 39 → 12. There is no other way to get this tail. Read with this hint, Deucalion's speech holds both cards: The World — "whatever both the East and the West behold"; The Moon — the clouds that "terrify my mind". A whole world and a night fear, added together, make a pause. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.
Among Waite's reversed meanings of The Hanged Man is "the crowd". In Latin, Deucalion says "nos duo turba sumus" — literally "we two are the crowd", the whole population of the earth.

sections.h2: The Tower — middle of the task: a house under lightning and towers under water
paragraphs: If 12-16-22 were a personal tail, its middle would come from its ends: 12 + 22 = 34 → 7, The Chariot. A couple's middle is the sum of the two partners' middles, and here it comes to 16 — The Tower. The Chariot is a vehicle steered by its own driver. The 12-16-22 couple gets no vehicle of its own: the road from wish to task runs through a collapse. In Ovid the two do not steer either — their boat is carried to the mountain.

The first Tower in the flood story is Lycaon's house, struck by lightning. Under that roof a guest was tested with a trap — that is, with deceit. "Deception" and "ruin" are in Waite's list of meanings for The Tower, and Waite himself calls the card the ruin of a "House of Falsehood". After Lycaon's house everything else goes under water, and Ovid names the drowned towers separately.

paragraphs.h3: It is not the couple's house that falls, but the world around it

paragraphs: Deucalion and Pyrrha built nothing on deceit, and it is not their house that falls. They walk across a land where the old order has ended: the temple of Themis still stands, but its roof "was defiled with foul moss", and its "altars were standing without fires". This is what the middle of this tail looks like. The couple makes its way through the ruins of a way of life that existed before it and without it: parents' rules, other people's expectations, plans once made for both of them. And the image formed at the start falls too — Lisovskaya lists the collapse of an invented image of the partner among the tasks of The Tower.

Lisovskaya's key to The Tower in a couple is that trials passed together make the union stronger. Among its minuses she notes that in hard times the partners look in different directions. Deucalion and Pyrrha look at the same empty land, and Ovid gives it a single line: "He thus spoke, and they wept." Deucalion says the same in his own words: "the marriage tie has united to me, and… now dangers themselves unite to me". The Tower in the middle of the tail is not the end of the union but a new knot.

paragraphs.h3: The letter that has to fall

paragraphs: The subtlest Tower in this story is the oracle. To "throw behind your backs the bones of your great mother", taken literally, means to desecrate a grave. Pyrrha hears the letter of it and freezes. Deucalion looks for a second meaning and finds it: "The earth is the great mother; I suspect that the stones in the body of the earth are the bones meant." To move on, the couple needs the literal reading of an old rule to collapse.

In the myth the roles are divided this way; in a living couple they change places: today one holds on to the letter, tomorrow the other. The difference in outlook that Lisovskaya puts among The Tower's minuses works as a plus here: without the second reading, the two would still be standing at the temple.

Wen assigns Water to The Hanged Man, Fire to The Tower and Air to The Fool. In Ovid's first book the world goes through all three elements in a single episode: the fire of the lightning over Lycaon's house, the water of the flood, and the north wind Aquilo, which Jupiter sends to drive away the clouds. The fourth element, earth, ends up in the couple's hands — as stones.
In Wen's reversed Tower there are these words as well: "Not all will be destroyed. There will be mercy and some will be saved." In Ovid, two are saved.

sections.h2: The Fool — main task: "But what harm will it do to try?"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task, and Lisovskaya reads it mostly through its minus: what the two cannot manage and what they need to learn. Her key to The Fool is freedom: in the plus it is the trust that gives freedom, in the minus it is a lack of boundaries and responsibility.

Here is Ovid's most Fool-like line: "Although she, descended from Titan, is moved by this interpretation of her husband, still her hope is involved in doubt; so much do they both distrust the advice of heaven; but what harm will it do to try?" No knowledge, no promise, no certainty that the reading is right — only the decision to try. And at once: "They go down, and they veil their heads, and ungird their garments, and cast stones, as ordered, behind their footsteps." The heads are covered — the two cannot see what will come of it. The belts are loosened — what held them tight is slack. The stones fly behind their backs, and looking round is not allowed.

paragraphs.h3: Testing the other, or trying it themselves

paragraphs: This book has two experiments. Lycaon enjoys "this mode of testing the truth": he tests his guest with a trap, and his house falls. Deucalion and Pyrrha try for themselves, with their own hands, and the world comes back. In the Latin, Lycaon says "experiar", "I will test", and the last line of the episode calls the people born from the stones — that is, all of us — "experiens laborum", tried in labours. Waite writes of The Fool: "He is the spirit in search of experience." The main task of the 12-16-22 couple is to choose the second kind of experiment.

This bears directly on The Fool's minus in a couple. Lisovskaya describes control and jealousy from someone who does not keep their own rules, and advises giving the partner freedom without checks. In Ovid, checking up on the other stands at the start of the collapse. Trust that is stronger than doubt stands at the start of a new world.

paragraphs.h3: An easy start and a serious step

paragraphs: The Fool is good at beginnings. After any collapse, a 12-16-22 couple can pack everything into one bag and leave, change everything, start on bare ground — Lisovskaya counts this as a plus: they start from zero with ease. The minus sits in the same place: the start is easy, and the serious step gets put off. In words everything is settled, yet a shared address, a shared account or a shared "we" never arrives. Each lives their own life, and the couple comes to resemble two neighbours.

In Ovid the serious step is taken, but not at once: first a refusal, then a long silence, then a word of doubt, and only then the throw. Ovid notes: "they reconsider the words of the response given, but involved in dark obscurity, and they ponder them among themselves." The couple's task is neither to leap over this doubt nor to drown in it, but to get as far as the throw.

paragraphs.h3: Who are we to each other now

paragraphs: Deucalion addresses Pyrrha by three names at once — sister (a cousin, in fact), wife, the only woman left in the world — and lists three bonds: shared blood, marriage, and now danger. The old words are not enough after the flood, so he adds a new one. Among The Fool's minuses, Lisovskaya lists an undefined status of the relationship. After The Tower, the old names for a 12-16-22 couple's bond may stop fitting — and the main task includes a simple thing: to say aloud who the two are to each other now.

Deucalion dreams of doing what his father once did: "Oh that I could replace the people that are lost by the arts of my father, and infuse the soul into the moulded earth!" Prometheus moulded people from earth. That way is closed to his son, and the new world comes about differently — by the throw of two people, not by the craft of one master. The Fool does not inherit a method; he finds his own. The 12-16-22 couple builds its life not by its parents' recipe, however good.

And one more detail. The stones do not become people at once: they "began to lay aside their hardness and their stiffness, and by degrees to become soft", and then they look "as if from the marble commenced to be wrought, not sufficiently distinct, and very like to rough statues". What this couple starts is rough and unfinished at first, and that is normal. "There is no delay," Ovid says of the people themselves, while it is the stones that change slowly. The Hanged Man's pause does not vanish; it passes from the people into the work.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: a hope that neither of the two has
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is its shared atmosphere: what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In couples with the 12-16-22 tail, the centre always holds 17, The Star. No birth date gives 17 in the centre of a personal chart, so this hope belongs to neither partner. It appears only when there are two.

paragraphs.h3: Why The Fool and The Star make The Hanged Man

paragraphs: In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. This couple keeps the rule: 22 + 17 = 39 → 12. The Fool plus The Star is The Hanged Man. Read as a hint, the equation says this couple's pause is made not of fear but of its freedom and its hope. The two wait not because they are afraid to step, but because there is something inside them worth waiting for the right moment. This is our reading of the arithmetic. The weak version of the same equation is a waiting in which freedom and hope never turn into a step.

The couple's Star is made of two personal centres, the way Parnassus is made of two summits — "a lofty mountain rises towards the stars, with two tops". Neither summit reaches the stars alone. In 56% of these couples it is Justice (8) and The Hermit (9), in 42% The Hanged Man (12) and The Hierophant (5), in 2% The Empress (3) and Temperance (14). Curiously, Ovid begins his portrait of the two with justice: "No man was there more upright than he, nor a greater lover of justice", and the advice they receive comes from Themis, the goddess of justice. This is a coincidence of images, not a law of the method.

According to Apollodorus, Pyrrha is "the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, the first woman fashioned by the gods". In Hesiod's Works and Days, Pandora opens the jar and troubles scatter over the world. "Only Hope remained there in an unbreakable home within under the rim of the great jar, and did not fly out at the door" (translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White). Inside, in an unbreakable home — while houses fall all over the earth. The centre of the chart is exactly that inside: the couple's Star lives where the collapse of the middle card cannot reach.

At the decisive moment Ovid names the two after their fathers: "the son of Prometheus soothes the daughter of Epimetheus with these gentle words". In Greek, Prometheus means "forethought" and Epimetheus "afterthought"; in Hesiod, Epimetheus "took the gift, and afterwards, when the evil thing was already his, he understood." The 12-16-22 tail follows the same path: from The Hanged Man, whose list in Waite includes "circumspection", to The Fool, who steps first and understands later. The couple needs both kinds.

Waite gives The Star two upright lists at once: "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment" — and "hope and bright prospects". The empty earth after the flood is both lists at the same time. And Ovid promises no more than there is: "still her hope is involved in doubt". The Star in the centre does not promise an outcome; it is simply there.

The first thing the two do after the flood is take a little of the very water that destroyed the world and sprinkle it on their heads and clothes: "they have sprinkled the waters poured on their clothes and their heads". Ovid's flood is "the boundless range of the sea". Waite describes The Star as the Great Mother who passes her riches to the spheres below "in the measure that they can receive her influx". Water without measure drowns; water in measure brings life. The atmosphere inside a couple with this Star needs the same distinction: support in the amount the other can take in.

Wen links the reversed Star with tears, and its message is comfort: "There, there, don't cry." Deucalion begins his speech in tears, and his first thought is who would comfort Pyrrha if he were not there. Comfort here is the first form of hope. Lisovskaya describes The Star in a couple this way: often it is only together that people understand who they want to be. In Ovid the two understand it literally: humankind begins with the two of them.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: four cards of the Waite–Smith deck
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own artwork. This section is about the Waite–Smith deck (1909) and how Waite himself described it.

ul: **The Hanged Man.** The tree the figure hangs from is "living wood, with leaves thereon"; in the section on older versions of the card Waite writes that "the arms are bound behind him". The oracle tells the couple to do the opposite: to loosen their belts and throw stones behind their backs with their own hands.

**The Tower.** Lightning strikes the tower, the crown flies off, two figures fall. Waite explains them as "the literal word made void and the other its false interpretation" — exactly what falls at the temple of Themis. Among the card's old names he lists "God's House and the Tower of Babel".

**The Star.** A naked woman pours "Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land". "Her left knee is on the land and her right foot upon the water." After a flood in which "to that ocean shores were wanting", this figure separates water and land again — and she does it with two vessels.

**The Fool.** A young man at the edge of a precipice looks not down but at "its expanse of sky rather than the prospect below". Waite writes: "His countenance is full of intelligence and expectant dream." Not carelessness, but expectation.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values (its spiritual purpose) answer the question of what the union exists for. In 12-16-22 couples one of two cards stands here: The Lovers in 58.5%, The Devil in 41.5%.

**The Lovers** turn the main task into a choice. Wen compares The Fool's fork in the road with the choice of The Lovers: "in The Lovers card, the choice often has ethical undertones. With The Fool, the choice is not over ethics or morality; it is a choice between two forks in the path." For such a couple, a step into the unknown is not just a road but a decision to choose each other again. Deucalion does it aloud: first blood joined them, then marriage, now danger — and each time the bond is confirmed anew.

**The Devil** points to the chain hidden in the words "we only have each other". With nobody else around, it is easy to start holding on to a partner the way one holds on to a broken mast. Lisovskaya's final thought on The Devil is that nobody belongs to anybody. In Ovid, The Devil and The Tower stand side by side from the very beginning: Lycaon becomes a wolf, and his house falls to the lightning. Waite sets these cards against each other in the same way: The Devil is "the fall into the material and animal state", The Tower "destruction on the intellectual side". For a couple with The Devil in its values, the main thing is not to turn a saving closeness into captivity and not to hold on to what is dead, as Pyrrha holds on to her mother's bones.

sections.h2: How the 12-16-22 tail is formed: an example and three combinations
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the same points in two personal charts, reduced to 22. An example with the dates 07.01.1976 and 14.09.1975:

head: Point
Couple

paragraphs: The partners' personal tails are 21-7-13 and 18-9-9. Neither contains The Hanged Man, The Tower or The Fool: all three cards are born only in the sum.
The 12-16-22 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 215 (0.464%) and ranks 57th of the 97 couple tails. It comes from three combinations of personal tails:

ul: **18-9-9 + 21-7-13** — 56% of these couples (as in the example);

paragraphs: In all three, one partner brings The Moon into the shared entry and the other brings The World. By our count over all dates from 1900 to 2026, the personal tails 21-7-13, 21-10-16 and 21-10-7 together occur in about 3.3% of people, while 18-9-9, 18-6-6 and 18-6-15 occur in about 16.7%: the rare one in this couple is the partner with The World. In 42% of couples The Tower is in one partner's personal tail (21-10-16, as their main task), and the other partner has The Hanged Man in the centre of their personal chart. In the remaining couples both The Tower and The Hanged Man appear only in the sum. Neither The Fool nor The Star is found in any of the six personal tails: The Fool in this tail is born only in the couple, and so is The Star in the centre.

sections.h2: What the 12-16-22 tail asks of a couple
paragraphs: When Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail, she marks which combination of energies each conclusion comes from. The same is done here.

ul: **Do not mistake a pause for a decision** (12 + 22). There are always clouds in the sky; waiting until "everything is completely calm" can take years.
**Say what each one wants, not only what each one gives up** (12). The language of sacrifice is beautiful, but it has no wishes in it.
**Look in one direction when the familiar falls** (16). First grieve together, then ask together how to go on.
**Let go of the literal reading of old rules** (12 + 16). A parent's "that's how it's done" may have been right for a different world.
**Take the step with no safety net, but together** (22). Each throws their own stones; no one does it for the other.
**Give freedom without checks** (16 + 22). Testing his guest cost Lycaon his house.
**After the collapse, name the bond anew** (16 + 22). The old "we're just together" may no longer describe what there is.
**Allow the new to be rough** (12 + 16 + 22). Ovid's stones become people gradually.

paragraphs.h3: The weak and the strong version

paragraphs: In the weak version, the couple stays in the boat. Its common language is waiting and mutual sacrifice, decisions are postponed, and when the familiar falls, each lives through it alone. The Fool's freedom turns into flight from serious steps, or into the life of two neighbours under one roof.

In the strong version, the couple steps onto the shore. The two grieve together for what has fallen, read the old rules in a new way, name their bond anew and take a step that neither is fully sure of. Their new world looks at first like rough-hewn marble — and comes alive.

paragraphs.h3: Questions a couple can ask itself

ul: What is our "boat" right now — where are we waiting things out, though the water has already gone?
Which rule do we still read literally, though the world in which it was right has ended?
What do we call each other — and does that name fit what is between us?
Which stone is each of us ready to throw behind our back with our own hands?

**12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is pause and care: "let's wait it out", "I'll do it for you". This wish is how the couple enters its task, and the same wish turns into resistance: waiting feels safer than deciding.

**16, The Tower — middle of the task.** The road runs through a collapse. What falls is whatever stood on someone else's foundation: the old way of life, the rule "that's how it's done", the partner as first imagined.

**22, The Fool — main task.** To start again as two — with no safety net, no "must", each with their own hands. The difficulty lies in the serious step: not to run from it and not to freeze in front of it.

intro: This tail's story was written down two thousand years ago. In the first book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, two people are left on earth after the flood: Deucalion and Pyrrha. Their story moves in the same order as the cards, and it even contains a Star that neither of the two has alone.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 12-16-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task is The Hanged Man, the middle is The Tower and the main task is The Fool. The couple's common language is pause and care, the road runs through the collapse of an old way of life and old rules, and the main task is to start again as two, with no safety net and without running from serious steps. Every such couple has The Star in the centre.

faq.q: Does The Tower in a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events. The Tower in the middle describes a way of walking the path: through the collapse of whatever stood on someone else's foundation — a way of life, rules, invented images. Lisovskaya's key to The Tower in a couple is that trials passed together make the union stronger. In the myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha, the two stay together after the collapse.

faq.q: Why does no personal chart have the 12-16-22 tail?
faq.a: In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With a main task of 22, an entry of 12 needs a centre of 17, and no birth date gives The Star in the centre of a personal chart. The middle of a personal tail is also calculated from its ends and would give 7, while a couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles and equals 16.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 12-16-22 calculated?
faq.a: The same points of the two personal charts are added, and each sum is reduced to 22. For the dates 07.01.1976 and 14.09.1975: the entry is 21 + 18 = 39 → 12, the middle 7 + 9 = 16, the main task 13 + 9 = 22. The couple's centre is 8 + 9 = 17, The Star.

faq.q: Is there a couple's tail with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No: among the 97 couple tails, the numbers 12, 16 and 22 appear only in the order 12-16-22. The closest is the tail 12-7-22 — the same ends, with The Chariot in the middle: there the path from pause to freedom runs along a road rather than through a collapse.

This is how the middle of the tail is lived — among the ruins of a way of life that existed before the couple and without it: parents' rules, other people's expectations, plans once made for both, and the partner as first imagined.

The two look at the same empty land, and Ovid gives it a single line: "He thus spoke, and they wept." Deucalion says: "the marriage tie has united to me, and… now dangers themselves unite to me." The collapse in the middle of the tail is not the end of the union but a new knot.

The subtlest Tower is the oracle, which tells the two to throw the bones of their great mother behind their backs. Taken literally, this means desecrating a grave, and Pyrrha freezes. Deucalion finds a second reading: the great mother is the earth, her bones are stones. To move on, the literal reading of an old rule has to collapse. In the myth the roles are divided this way; in a living couple they change places: today one holds on to the letter, tomorrow the other.

report.h3: "But what harm will it do to try?"

report: The main task is The Fool, and here is Ovid's most Fool-like line: "still her hope is involved in doubt; so much do they both distrust the advice of heaven; but what harm will it do to try?" No knowledge, no promise — only the decision to try. The two cover their heads, loosen their belts and throw stones behind their backs without looking round.

This book has two experiments. Lycaon enjoys "this mode of testing the truth" — he tests his guest, and his house falls. Deucalion and Pyrrha try for themselves, with their own hands, and the world comes back. Waite calls The Fool "the spirit in search of experience". **The couple's main task is to choose the second kind of experiment:** freedom without checks.

The Fool's minus is that beginning is easy. After a collapse, such a couple can pack everything into one bag and start on bare ground, while the serious step gets put off. In words everything is settled, yet a shared address, a shared account or a shared "we" never arrives, and the two come to resemble neighbours. Deucalion addresses Pyrrha by three names at once — sister, wife, the only woman left in the world — and adds a new bond: danger. After The Tower the old names may stop fitting, and part of the task is to say aloud who the two are to each other now.

Ovid's stones do not become people at once: at first they look "as if from the marble commenced to be wrought, not sufficiently distinct, and very like to rough statues". "There is no delay," Ovid says of the people, while it is the stones that change slowly. **The Hanged Man's pause does not vanish; it passes from the people into the work.**

In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. This couple keeps the rule: The Fool and The Star together make The Hanged Man. Read as a hint, the couple's pause is made not of fear but of its freedom and its hope. The weak version is a waiting in which freedom and hope never turn into a step.

According to Apollodorus, Pyrrha's mother is Pandora. In Hesiod, when the troubles scatter from the jar, "only Hope remained there in an unbreakable home within under the rim of the great jar". Inside, in an unbreakable home — while houses fall all over the earth.

The first thing the two do after the flood is sprinkle their heads and clothes with the very water that destroyed the world. Ovid's flood is "the boundless range of the sea"; Waite describes The Star as a power that gives "in the measure that they can receive her influx". Water without measure drowns; water in measure brings life. In the strong version of the tail, the couple steps out of the boat onto the shore: it grieves together for what has fallen, reads the old rules in a new way and takes a step that neither of the two is fully sure of.
